title: True Crime: The Phantom of Heilbronn
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the Phantom of Heilbronn, a female serial offender linked by DNA to a string of murders, strangulations, burglaries and thefts across Germany, Austria, France and Luxembourg from 2001 to 2008. The case begins with the April 2007 murder of policewoman Michèle Kiesewetter in Heilbronn, and the hosts explain the early history of forensic DNA profiling, the 1997 discovery of trace DNA by Roland Van Oorschot, and the European DNA database treaties. The DNA trail led police to a woman nicknamed the Phantom, with clues including a heroin needle, a Roma connection, and a conflicting eyewitness description of a man with a soul patch. Police spent about 16,000 overtime hours and offered rewards, but the case collapsed in March 2009 when the DNA turned out to come from a Polish woman who worked at a cotton swab factory, Grinder Bio One International. The episode then covers the wider implications for forensic DNA, including contamination risks and rapid DNA machines, and the Nazi NSU cell that was later tied to Kiesewetter's murder. A listener mail segment about invasive species closes the episode.

segments.title: Opening and sponsor plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the episode, plug the Cooperative for Education donation drive, and introduce the Phantom of Heilbronn as a criminal mastermind case.

segments.title: History of forensic DNA profiling
segments.summary: The hosts trace DNA forensics from its 1980s UK origins, the Colin Pitchfork case, Alec Jeffreys' discovery, the FBI database, and Roland Van Oorschot's 1997 trace DNA work. They also cover European database treaties.

segments.title: Murder of policewoman Michèle Kiesewetter
segments.summary: In April 2007 policewoman Michèle Kiesewetter was shot in Heilbronn while on lunch break; her colleague Martin Arnold survived a coma with memory loss. DNA found in the patrol car matched a woman's profile, puzzling investigators.

segments.title: Linked cold cases and the woman without a face
segments.summary: Investigators linked the DNA to the 2001 strangling of Joseph Wallzenbach and the strangling of an elderly woman in a cold case, which led media to call the suspect the Woman Without a Face and the Phantom of Heilbronn.

segments.title: Petty crimes and a trail across Europe
segments.summary: The same DNA appeared at burglaries, car thefts, a toy pistol robbery in France, and a heroin needle. The hosts describe the suspect's suspected drug use, a Roma connection, and accomplices who stayed silent.

segments.title: Triple murder, soul patch witness, and identity limits
segments.summary: The DNA turned up in a 2008 triple murder of used car dealers in the Rhine, a 2006 attempted break-in with a witness describing a soul patch, and a fishing lodge robbery near Luxembourg. German laws limited ethnicity analysis, and a DNA dragnet of about 3,000 women found nothing.

segments.title: The collapse: cotton swab contamination
segments.summary: In March 2009 a DNA match to an asylum seeker proved impossible, and Stern magazine reported the phantom was DNA from a Polish woman working at a cotton swab factory, Grinder Bio One International. The company said its swabs were not for DNA collection.

segments.title: Lessons for forensic DNA and the NSU link
segments.summary: The hosts discuss DNA's limits, the CSI effect, a wrongful cab driver case, contamination control standards, rapid DNA machines, and the Golden State Killer. They also explain that the NSU Nazi cell was later tied to Kiesewetter's murder.

segments.title: Listener mail on invasive species
segments.summary: Eve from Libertyville, Illinois writes about shooting invasive plants in Maui with sharpshooters and helicopters, referencing the Select episode on invasive species.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck sign off and direct listeners to the podcast email address.
